title: NANO Nuclear and Quadrant Nuclear Industries Sign Memorandum of Understanding to Advance Domestic HALEU Fuel Supply
summary: Companies to explore long-term HALEU supply arrangement supporting advanced reactor deployments and strengthening the U.S. nuclear fuel supply chain New York, N.Y., and Boston, Massachusetts., Aug. 18, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- NANO Nuclear Energy Inc. (NASDAQ: NNE) (“NANO Nuclear” or “the Company”), a leading advanced nuclear micro modular reactor and technology company focused on developing […]
body_text: Companies to explore long-term HALEU supply arrangement supporting advanced reactor deployments and strengthening the U.S. nuclear fuel supply chain New York, N.Y., and Boston, Massachusetts., Aug. 18, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- NANO Nuclear Energy Inc. (NASDAQ: NNE) (“NANO Nuclear” or “the Company”) , a leading advanced nuclear micro modular reactor and technology company focused on developing clean energy solutions, and Quadrant Nuclear Industries, Inc. (QNI), a developer of integrated nuclear fuel cycle capabilities, today announced they have entered into a memorandum of understanding (MoU) establishing a non-binding framework for collaboration on the future supply of high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU) fuel. The MoU reflects a shared commitment to strengthening the domestic nuclear fuel supply chain, accelerating deployment of advanced reactors, including NANO Nuclear’s KRONOS MMR TM Energy System , and supporting U.S. energy security and decarbonization objectives. Under the MoU, NANO Nuclear and QNI will engage in discussions over the coming years regarding the potential supply and long-term offtake of HALEU produced at QNI's planned Vanguard facility at Idaho National Laboratory (INL). Figure 1 - NANO Nuclear Energy and Quadrant Nuclear Industries Sign Memorandum of Understanding to Advance Domestic HALEU Fuel Supply. "We are pleased to establish this MoU with QNI as we continue advancing our multi-pronged business plan, including development of our microreactor technologies and future deployment strategies," said James Walker, CEO of NANO Nuclear Energy . "Access to reliable, domestically produced HALEU will be a key element in supporting the growth of advanced nuclear energy. We look forward to collaborating with QNI as we evaluate additional fuel supply options that can enhance flexibility and strengthen the resilience of our long-term commercialization strategy." "Reliable nuclear fuel supply is one of the critical enablers of advanced reactor deployment," said Dee Mewbourne, CEO of QNI. "Our MoU with NANO Nuclear reflects the importance of connecting fuel production with reactor development early in the development and commercialization process. Together, we are helping build the supply chain foundation needed to support the next generation of nuclear energy." QNI is developing an integrated HALEU production capability in coordination with the U.S. Department of Energy and other key stakeholders. Its planned Vanguard facility at INL is designed to produce up to eighteen metric tons of HALEU annually at full capacity, supporting both commercial and government markets for advanced nuclear reactors. The companies intend to collaborate on areas including fuel supply planning, technical interface requirements, commercial structuring, regulatory coordination, logistics considerations, and demand forecasting associated with future HALEU supply arrangements. This collaboration provides a foundation for potential commercial agreements as both companies advance their respective development programs. For Full Official Press Release Press Here

The 2027 Toyota bZ reflects Toyota’s ongoing approach to electrification: useful range, accessible charging, everyday comfort, and a driving experience that inspires confidence. It plays a central role in Toyota’s commitment to electrification, giving customers an EV that fits seamlessly into real life. It is also part of Toyota’s multi-pathway approach to electrification as one of three BEV models that reside alongside 15 hybrid and two plug-in hybrid models, offering customers a variety of electrified vehicle options to best fit their needs. At the heart of the bZ is Toyota’s continued focus on real-world usability. Among its all-electric driving range options are the feature-packed Limited AWD model with a manufacturer-estimated 278-mile total driving range rating or the go-the-distance XLE FWD Plus with a manufacturer-estimated total driving range rating of 314 miles. Available battery sizes include a 74.7-kWh unit on the XLE AWD and FWD Plus, Limited AWD and FWD models, and a 57.7-kWh unit on the XLE FWD model. The bZ is equipped with the North American Charging System (NACS) for access to most high-speed chargers across America. The 2027 bZ also has battery preconditioning to help make high-speed charging more seamless in a variety of conditions. The 2027 bZ models are expected to start arriving at Toyota dealerships this September. The Manufacturer’s Suggested Retail Price will start at $34,980 (XLE FWD), excluding Dealer Processing and Handling fee, click here for full line pricing. * Driving ranges will vary depending on speed, outside temperature, accessory use, how/where you drive, charging habits, and other factors Exterior Features: Electrifying Style The 2027 Toyota bZ features a sleek exterior that emphasizes a low and planted stance. Its front-end design delivers a sleek, contemporary look with a hammerhead hood and standard LED light bar. While available details such as distinctive wheel treatments, black accents, and available two-tone styling help differentiate grades and personalize the vehicle’s appearance. It also has a color keyed front center bumper, thin lower grille, and rear spoiler, standard. Color matched overfenders are also available. There is privacy glass on all rear side, quarter, and liftgate windows for added privacy. The overall result is an electric SUV with a polished, aerodynamic profile that looks purpose-built for the modern era while remaining unmistakably Toyota. Interior Features: Spacious, Modern, and Driver-Focused Inside, the 2027 bZ presents a clean, contemporary cabin with a horizontal dashboard design and a strong emphasis on usability. A standard 14-inch Toyota Audio Multimedia display anchors the interior, while available premium touches add comfort and refinement throughout the cabin. Thoughtful details include standard dual wireless charging, front and rear interior ambient lighting with 64 available colors, dual zone climate control, and heated front seats. Premium climate amenities, like heated and ventilated front seats, heated rear seats, and front radiant foot-and-leg heaters are standard on the Limited grade models. Seating materials are available in SofTex® with fabric mixed media trim or SofTex trim, depending on grade. Passenger and cargo space are practical for everyday use, with 42.1 inches of front legroom, 35.3 inches of rear legroom, and 27.7 cubic feet of cargo volume behind the second row (without subwoofer). The rear cargo area has 56.9 cubic feet of space with the second row down (without subwoofer). Interior and Exterior Colors: Expressive Style The 2027 bZ’s sleek design and tech-forward cabin have the following available exterior colors: Wind Chill Pearl (Extra cost color) Wind Chill Pearl with Midnight Black Metallic Roof (Limited grade only; Extra cost color) Supersonic Red (Extra cost color) Supersonic Red with Midnight Black Metallic Roof (Limited grade only; Extra cost color) Blueprint Midnight Black Metallic Heavy Metal (Extra cost color) Heavy Metal with Midnight Black Metallic Roof (Limited grade only; Extra cost color) Interior colors vary by grade as follows: XLE: Black SofTex/fabric mixed media trim Limited: Black SofTex trim or Light Gray SofTex trim Driving Dynamics: Smooth, Responsive, and Confident The Toyota bZ delivers electric driving that feels composed and responsive. Toyota’s compact, lightweight and energy-efficient eAxles use silicon carbide semiconductors to help deliver thrilling output while maximizing range. Front-wheel-drive models produce either 165 total system horsepower (XLW FWD grade) or 221 total system horsepower (XLW FWD Plus and Limited FWD), while available all-wheel-drive models deliver up to 338 total system horsepower, giving the bZ strong acceleration and confident passing power. Toyota engineers have also tuned the bZ for a refined ride and stable handling. Toyota’s BEV-dedicated e-TNGA platform supports a low center of gravity and a rigid foundation by placing the battery pack flat under the floor. Combined with the battery cross-framing structure, lightweight body construction and dynamic suspension, the architecture is intended to enhance ride quality, stability and handling precision. Available all-wheel-drive capability adds traction in challenging weather and road conditions, reinforcing the bZ’s versatility as a daily-driver EV. Additional driving-related features include: Steering wheel-mounted paddle shifters to adjust regenerative braking X-MODE on AWD models for selectable traction optimization Grip-Control for low-speed assistance in adverse conditions on AWD models Intelligent throttle tuning for smoother acceleration and deceleration Vehicle Stability Control to help maintain vehicle control in adverse conditions BEV System: Charged Up for Daily Driving The 2027 bZ has a standard North American Charging System (NACS) port. Under ideal conditions, DC fast charging can replenish the battery from 10% to 80% in approximately 30 minutes.** The model also has Plug & Charge*** capability, which helps streamline the charging experience at supported networks. It can also use Level 1 and Level 2 power sources to charge and includes a standard dual-voltage charging cable. Each bZ model also has a standard adapter kit for compatibility with SAE J1772 and Combined Charging System (CCS) stations, providing even greater charging convenience and flexibility. The 2027 bZ offers a variety of manufacturer estimated electric driving ranges and two battery options: 314 miles — XLE FWD Plus, 74.7-kWh battery** 299 miles — Limited FWD, 74.7-kWh battery** 288 miles — XLE AWD, 74.7-kWh battery** 299 miles — Limited AWD, 74.7-kWh battery** 236 miles — XLE FWD, 57.7-kWh battery** ** Driving ranges and charging times will vary depending on speed, outside temperature, accessory use, how/where you drive, charging habits, and other factors ***Certain functionality of Plug and Charge requires a Remote Connect trial or subscription. 4G Network dependent. Key Features by Grade XLE The XLE serves as the foundation of the lineup with essential EV capability and a strong set of standard features, including: 14-inch Toyota Audio Multimedia display LED lighting 18-inch alloy wheels Heated front seats and steering wheel Dual-zone climate control SofTex-trimmed and fabric mixed media seating Limited The Limited grade models add premium available features such as: 20-inch alloy wheels Panoramic fixed-glass moonroof Heated and ventilated front seats Heated rear seats SofTex-trimmed seating Digital rearview mirror Toyota Audio Multimedia System & Connected Technology The 2027 Toyota bZ has a standard 14-inch touchscreen featuring the Toyota Audio Multimedia system, developed by the Texas-based Toyota Connected North America team. The system has six-speakers, standard, and supports wireless Apple CarPlay® and Android Auto™. A JBL® premium audio system with 9-speakers (including subwoofer) and amplifier is optional on the Limited grade models. Interior tech features include standard dual Qi® wireless charging with enhanced power output, multiple USB-C ports, and a 120V/1500W AC outlet in the rear cargo area. It has a top-mount Multi-Information Display (MID) with indicators and 7-inch customizable LCD display with speedometer, charge meter, power output meter, drive mode indicators, charging information and more. The 2027 bZ includes 5-year trials for Safety Connect****, Service Connect****, and Remote Connect**** and a 30 day/3 GB Wi-Fi Connect**** trial. Additional services, such as Drive Connect*****, are available depending on grade, visit Toyota Connected Services to learn more. All bZ models are also Toyota Digital Key capable, which enables a smartphone to be used instead of a physical key (Remote Connect subscription required). Owners can also use the Toyota App, with an active Remote Connect subscription or trial; they can check charging status, start or stop charging, locate nearby charging stations and manage remote vehicle functions. ****4G network dependent, subscription required after trial. ***** Requires a Remote Connect trial or subscription. 4G Network dependent. Safety & Convenience All 2027 bZ models come standard with Toyota Safety Sense 3.0, Toyota’s suite of active safety and convenience systems. This suite of features includes: Pre-Collision System with Pedestrian Detection Full-Speed Range Dynamic Radar Cruise Control Lane Departure Alert with Steering Assist Lane Tracing Assist Road Sign Assist Automatic High Beams Proactive Driving Assist Additional standard safety features include: Blind Spot Monitor with Rear Cross-Traffic Alert Safe Exit Alert Toyota Star Safety System The Limited grade models also have Traffic Jam Assist******, Lane Change Assist, Front Cross-Traffic Alert and a Panoramic View Monitor with Perimeter Scan. ******Requires a Remote Connect trial or subscription. 4G Network dependent. Limited Warranty Toyota’s 36-month/36,000-mile basic new-vehicle warranty applies to all components other than normal wear and maintenance items. Additional 60-month warranties cover the powertrain for 60,000 miles and corrosion with no mileage limitation. The Electric Vehicle Driving Components, including the traction battery, are covered for 8 years or 100,000 miles, whichever comes first. Toyota dealers have complete details on the limited warranty. The Toyota bZ also comes with ToyotaCare, a plan covering normal factory-scheduled maintenance, for one year or 10,000 miles, whichever comes first, and three years of Roadside Assistance, regardless of mileage. title: SAT Scores for Colleges: 2026 Guide to Ranges & Policies
summary: Your 2026 guide to SAT scores for colleges: tiers, mid-50% ranges, and test-required lists. Set targets and know when to submit your score.
body_text: SAT Scores for Colleges: 2026 Guide to Ranges & Policies TL;DR The average SAT score is 1029 out of 1600, but “good” is entirely relative to the colleges on your list. Ivy League and top-20 schools expect scores in the 1490 to 1580 range, competitive state flagships cluster around 1200 to 1400, and most four-year colleges admit students scoring between 1050 and 1200. More than 90% of colleges remain test-optional for 2026, but a growing wave of elite schools (Harvard, MIT, Yale, Stanford, and others) now require the SAT or ACT again. Understanding SAT scores for colleges is one of the most practical things a student can do before building a college list. But the terminology is confusing, the policies keep shifting, and most guides either drown you in data tables or give you a vague “it depends.” This guide is different. It defines every term you need to know, gives you concrete score benchmarks by college tier, and explains the strategic decisions that turn a score into an admissions advantage. If you want to see where you stand right now, take a free SAT practice test before reading further. Having a baseline score makes everything below more actionable. Quick Answer: What SAT Score Do You Need for College? College Type Competitive SAT Score Ivy League and Top 10 1490-1580 Top 20-50 Universities 1350-1530 State Flagship Universities 1200-1400 Four-Year Colleges 1050-1200 Open Admission Colleges Below 1050 The right SAT score depends on the colleges on your list. A 1200 is competitive at many public universities, a 1400 is strong for most selective colleges, and a 1500+ places you among applicants to Ivy League and top-10 schools. More than 90% of colleges remain test-optional in 2026, but many elite universities have reinstated testing requirements. What Are SAT Scores? The Basics The SAT is scored on a scale of 400 to 1600. That total, called your composite score, is the sum of two section scores: Evidence-Based Reading and Writing (200 to 800) and Math (200 to 800). For the class of 2025, the national average composite was 1029 , with an average Reading and Writing score of 521 and an average Math score of 508. Over 2 million students took the test, the first class to clear that mark since 2020. Here’s something that matters more than the average: only 39% of test-takers met both college readiness benchmarks , down from 45% before the pandemic. The typical SAT score is lower than most families assume. How the Digital SAT’s Adaptive System Affects Your Score Since the SAT went fully digital in 2023, it uses a multistage adaptive format. You complete Module 1, and based on your performance, the system routes you to either a harder or easier Module 2. This matters because if you’re routed to the easier second module, your maximum possible section score is effectively capped around 600 to 650. The test rewards strong starts. SAT Score Terms at a Glance Term Definition Composite Score Your total SAT score Superscore Combining your best section scores Middle 50% The 25th-75th percentile range Score Choice Choosing which scores to send Test-Optional Score submission is optional Glossary of SAT Score Terms These are the terms you’ll encounter when researching SAT scores for colleges. Each definition includes a brief explanation of why it matters for admissions. Composite Score Your total SAT score, the sum of your Reading & Writing section score and your Math section score. Range: 400 to 1600. This is the number colleges cite most often and the one you’ll compare against published score ranges. Section Score Your individual score on either the Reading & Writing section or the Math section, each ranging from 200 to 800. Some engineering-heavy programs weigh Math more heavily, while humanities programs may pay closer attention to Reading & Writing. Knowing your section breakdown helps you target weak areas more efficiently. Percentile Rank The percentage of test-takers who scored at or below your score. A 75th percentile score means you outperformed 75% of students. But here’s a confusion point most guides skip: there are actually two percentile scales on your score report. User Percentile compares you only to students who actually sat for the SAT. Nationally Representative Percentile compares you to the entire U.S. high school population, including students who never took the test. A composite of 1200 sits at roughly the 74th Nationally Representative percentile but only the 57th to 59th User percentile . That’s a meaningful gap. When a college says “75th percentile,” they’re typically referring to admitted-student score distributions, not either of these scales. Middle 50% (Interquartile Range) The score band between a college’s 25th and 75th percentile of admitted students. If a school lists a middle 50% of 1350 to 1520, that means half of admitted students scored in that range. The other half is split: 25% scored below 1350, and 25% scored above 1520. Students constantly mistake the 25th percentile as a hard minimum. It isn’t. One in four admitted students scored below it. The middle 50% is a targeting tool, not a cutoff. Superscore The combination of your highest Reading & Writing score from one test date and your highest Math score from another. Most colleges, including most test-required ones, accept superscores. This changes the calculus on retaking the SAT. If you scored 720 Math but only 650 Reading & Writing on your first attempt, you can retake the test focused primarily on improving Reading & Writing, and the college will combine your best sections. For more on building a retake strategy, the SAT study schedule guide breaks down how to plan focused prep. Score Choice A College Board policy that lets you choose which test date’s scores to send to colleges. If you took the SAT three times and bombed the second sitting, you can send only your first and third scores. Note: some schools (like Georgetown) require all scores, so always check individual policies. College Readiness Benchmarks Thresholds set by the College Board (480 for Reading & Writing, 530 for Math) indicating a 75% likelihood of earning at least a C in first-year college courses. These aren’t admissions standards. They’re predictive indicators. Most competitive colleges expect scores well above these thresholds. Equating A statistical process that ensures a 1200 earned in March means the same thing as a 1200 earned in October, even though the questions are different. You don’t need to worry about “easier” or “harder” test dates. The College Board adjusts for difficulty so scores remain comparable across administrations. Test-Required vs. Test-Optional vs. Test-Free Three distinct admissions policies: Test-required : You must submit SAT or ACT scores. No exceptions. Test-optional : You choose whether to submit scores. The college considers them if sent but won’t penalize you for withholding. Test-free (or test-blind) : The college won’t consider test scores even if you send them. Very few schools operate this way. The category a school falls into directly shapes your application strategy, which we’ll cover in detail below. SAT Score Ranges by College Tier: 2026 Benchmarks When people search for SAT scores for colleges, they usually want a simple answer: what score do I need for schools at X level? The table below organizes the answer into five tiers, based on published middle 50% data from the most recent admissions cycle. Tier 1: Ivy League and Top 10 (Middle 50%: 1490 to 1580) These are the schools where almost every admitted student scores 1500 or above. Harvard admits students in the 1500 to 1580 range , MIT clusters between 1520 and 1570, and Stanford between 1510 and 1570. Yale, Princeton, Columbia, Penn, and Northwestern fall between 1470 and 1570. Caltech and Rice sit in similar territory. Only about 7% of all test-takers score between 1400 and 1600 , which gives you a sense of how concentrated the competition is at this level. Tier 2: Top 20 to 50 Selective (Middle 50%: 1350 to 1530) Schools like UCLA (1290 to 1510), UC Berkeley (1340 to 1540), Georgetown, Vanderbilt (1510 to 1560), and similar universities. A 1400 puts you solidly in range for most of these schools, and a 1500+ makes you competitive at the top end. Tier 3: Competitive State Flagships (Middle 50%: 1200 to 1400) Ohio State, Penn State, University of Michigan, UT Austin, and similar public universities. A score of 1200 or above, which is roughly the 75th percentile nationally , makes you competitive at most of these schools. Tier 4: Mid-Range Four-Year Colleges (Middle 50%: 1050 to 1200) Most state universities and many private colleges. Towson University, for example, admits students between 1020 and 1320 . At this tier, a score near or above 1100 is typically solid. Tier 5: Open or Broad Admission (Below 1050) Community colleges and open-enrollment universities. Many don’t require the SAT at all. Important caveat about score inflation : Published middle 50% ranges at test-optional schools are inflated. Why? Because only students with high scores tend to submit them. Practitioners on Reddit’s r/ApplyingToCollege frequently point this out, noting that the reported ranges overstate the actual competitiveness floor. A user-compiled thread ranking colleges by highest median SAT (which ranked in the top 15 of Google results for this query) makes the same observation. The published mid-50% SAT range at most Ivy League schools has climbed roughly 50 points at the 25th percentile since 2018-2019 , partly because of this self-selection effect. To gauge where you’d fall within these tiers, a score predictor can estimate your likely SAT score based on practice performance. What Colleges Can You Get Into With Your SAT Score? SAT Score Typical College Matches 1000 Regional public universities, many four-year colleges 1100 Mid-range public universities 1200 Competitive state universities 1300 Strong state flagships and selective private colleges 1400 Top 50 universities 1500+ Ivy League and top-20 universities Important: These are not admission guarantees. GPA, course rigor, extracurricular activities, essays, and recommendation letters still play a significant role. Test-Optional vs. Test-Required: Does Your SAT Score Still Matter? The short answer: yes, for most applicants. The Reinstatement Wave The test-optional era is narrowing at the top. More than 90% of ranked four-year colleges still don’t require scores for fall 2026 , but the list of elite schools bringing testing back grows every few months. For 2026 admissions, test-required schools include MIT, Harvard, Yale, Dartmouth, Stanford, Brown, Caltech, Georgetown, Purdue, the University of Tennessee, the University of Florida system, the University of Georgia, and all military service academies. Columbia, which had been the only Ivy publicly committed to permanent test-optional admissions, reversed course in June 2026 and will require the SAT or ACT starting with the 2027-2028 cycle. Princeton remains test-optional for current applicants but has already announced that scores will be required again starting with the Fall 2028 entering class. The rationale behind these reversals is worth noting. Dartmouth’s reversal was one of the most consequential because it argued that test-optional admissions had actually made it easier to overlook strong applicants from less-resourced backgrounds, students whose test scores would have been an asset when considered in context. Ohio State cited higher GPAs and retention rates among test submitters as justification for its own reinstatement. These are equity and predictive-validity arguments, not just selectivity plays. Colleges That Require SAT or ACT Scores in 2026 College Testing Policy Harvard Required MIT Required Yale Required Stanford Required Brown Required Dartmouth Required Caltech Required Georgetown Required Purdue Required University of Florida Required University of Georgia Required Military academies Required When to Submit vs. Withhold “Optional” describes the submission decision, not the weight. At selective test-optional schools, a submitted score above the school’s 75th percentile is a meaningful positive signal. A practical rule: submit if your score falls within or above a school’s published middle 50% range. Strongly submit if you’re at or above the 75th percentile. Withhold if you’re significantly below the 25th percentile. If you’re an international, homeschooled, or non-traditional student, submitting is generally more helpful because admissions committees have fewer standardized data points to evaluate your academic preparation. Most schools accept either the SAT or ACT, so consider whether a different test format suits you better. If the ACT’s structure feels more natural, ACT prep resources can help you compare. Should You Submit Your SAT Score? Your Score Recommendation Above the 75th percentile Definitely submit Within the middle 50% Usually submit Slightly below the 25th percentile Case by case Well below the 25th percentile Consider withholding How to Find SAT Score Ranges for Any College You don’t need to rely on third-party lists. Here’s how to find the data yourself: Check the school’s Common Data Set (CDS). Search “[School Name] Common Data Set” and look for Section C (First-Time, First-Year Admissions). The 25th and 75th percentile SAT scores are listed in a standard format. Visit the school’s admissions page. Most publish a “class profile” or “admitted student profile” with score ranges. Use College Board’s BigFuture. Search any school and see reported score distributions. When reading these reports, look for the 25th and 75th percentile columns. The 25th percentile is the score below which 25% of admitted students fell. The 75th percentile is the score above which only 25% of admits scored. And remember the inflation warning: at test-optional schools, these numbers reflect only students who chose to submit. The actual score distribution of enrolled students is broader than what’s published. How to Set Your Target SAT Score A vague goal like “I want a good score” doesn’t work. Here’s how to set a specific one. Step 1: Build your college list. Include reaches, targets, and safeties. Step 2: Find the highest 75th percentile score among your reach schools. That’s your goal. If your top-choice school’s 75th percentile is 1520, aim for 1520. Step 3: Take a diagnostic to find your starting point. The gap between your current level and your target determines how much prep you need and where to focus. A diagnostic and study plan will map out which skills need the most work. If you’re looking at a 200-point improvement, the guide to improving by 200 points breaks down a concrete plan. Step 4: Factor in scholarship thresholds. Many merit scholarship programs have specific SAT cutoffs that are separate from admissions score ranges. A student who scores 1400 might get admitted to a school but miss a scholarship that required 1450. The ROI on an extra few weeks of prep can be thousands of dollars in financial aid. How Much Does a Higher SAT Score Matter? Score Increase Potential Impact +50 points Stronger application +100 points More competitive admissions +150 points Additional scholarship opportunities +200 points Access to a higher admissions tier This reinforces your existing argument with clearer visuals. Step 5: Plan around superscoring. If your Math score is already strong but Reading & Writing is lagging, a targeted retake focused on one section can be more time-efficient than restudying everything. Most colleges will combine your best sections across sittings. Targeted SAT problem sets can help you drill specific weaknesses without redoing material you’ve already mastered. SAT Scores and Merit Scholarships Many colleges separate admissions requirements from scholarship requirements. SAT Score Scholarship Impact 1200 Some institutional scholarships 1300 Many merit scholarship programs 1400 Competitive merit awards 1500+ Maximum merit consideration at many universities Always check individual scholarship criteria because scholarship cutoffs often differ from admissions benchmarks. SAT Percentiles vs. College Competitiveness Percentile Approximate SAT College Competitiveness 99th 1500+ Ivy League 90th 1400 Top 50 75th 1300 State flagship 50th 1050 Four-year colleges The Score Distribution You Should Know To put SAT scores for colleges into perspective, here’s how the roughly 2 million class-of-2025 test-takers were distributed: Score Range Approximate Percentile (User) What It Means 1500+ ~99th percentile Competitive for Ivy League and top 10 1400 to 1490 ~93rd to 98th Strong for top-20 to top-50 schools 1200 to 1390 ~74th to 92nd Competitive for most state flagships 1050 to 1190 ~50th to 73rd Solid for many four-year colleges Below 1050 Below 50th Below the national average The key thresholds worth memorizing: 1510 for the top 5%, 1460 for the top 10%, and 1310 for the top 25% on the User percentile scale. Frequently Asked Questions What is the average SAT score? The national average for the class of 2025 was 1029 out of 1600. By section, it was 521 Reading & Writing and 508 Math. What SAT score do I need for Ivy League schools? Most Ivy League schools admit students in the 1470 to 1580 range (middle 50%). Harvard, Yale, and Princeton have 25th percentiles at or above 1500. A score below 1480 is now below the 25th percentile at all three. Do all colleges require the SAT in 2026? No. Over 90% of ranked four-year colleges remain test-optional for fall 2026 admissions, and over 1,000 colleges on the Common App are test-optional. However, a growing number of elite schools (including Harvard, MIT, Yale, Stanford, Brown, Dartmouth, Caltech, and Georgetown) now require scores. Should I submit my SAT score to a test-optional school? Submit if your score is within or above the school’s published middle 50% range. If your score falls well below the 25th percentile, withholding is usually the better strategy. What is a superscore, and do colleges accept it? A superscore combines your highest Reading & Writing score from one test date with your highest Math score from another. Most colleges accept superscores, which makes retaking the SAT strategically valuable even if only one section needs improvement. Can I retake the SAT to improve my score? Yes. The SAT is offered 8 times per year. There’s no limit on retakes, and with Score Choice, you can control which scores colleges see. Most admissions counselors recommend two to three attempts. How is the digital SAT scored differently from the old paper test? The digital SAT uses multistage adaptive modules. Your performance on Module 1 determines whether Module 2 is harder or easier. If you’re routed to the easier Module 2, your maximum section score is capped around 600 to 650. The scoring scale (400 to 1600) and section structure (two sections, 200 to 800 each) remain the same. Does a 1300 SAT score get me into a good college? It depends entirely on your college list. A 1300 is roughly the 87th percentile nationally, which is above average at many strong public universities and private colleges. It would be below the middle 50% at most top-25 schools. The only meaningful definition of a “good” score is one that meets or exceeds the expectations of the specific colleges you’re applying to. Knowing what SAT scores colleges expect is only useful if you know where you stand and have a plan to close the gap. If you haven’t already, start with a diagnostic to see your current score, identify your weakest areas, and build a personalized study path from there.
